metadata.title: AI Status Reports: Trust, but Verify
metadata.creator: Sanjana Rao
metadata.note: ai-explainer CONCEPT explainer for @HumanitariansAI, first-person Sanjana Rao (af_bella). Topic: trusting AI-generated project status reports. Framework = THE SIGN-OFF: AI drafts, you sign; verify SOURCED / CURRENT / COMPLETE before it reaches a stakeholder.

skin_warnings: T09: palette=claude but the outro is 'un-annotated' — OUTRO LAW wants ClaudeTitleOutro

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- ClaudeComposerAsk, ask answered; first-person Sanjana
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sanjana, a project manager at Humanitarians AI. Here's something that's quietly become normal: the AI in your project tools will now write your status report for you. One click, and out comes a clean paragraph you can send to your boss or your client. It sounds great. But a status report has your name on it. So the real question isn't whether the AI can write it. It's whether you can trust what it wrote -- before you hit send.

props.command: The AI in my project tools can auto-write a status report for my stakeholders. How do I know I can trust it before I send it?
output: AI can draft the status -- it reads your board fast
but it's only as true as the board behind it
verify three things before you sign and send

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW -- hesitant-writer BLUF; corrects the reel's real misconception
beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one breath. It's tempting to treat the AI's status report as the status itself. It isn't. It's a draft built only from what's on your board -- and a confident paragraph can hide an empty or stale one. Your job is to verify it before you sign it.

props.text:
The AI's status report is the status.
If it says on track, we're on track.
props.triggerWords: is the status, If it says on track, we're on track
props.replacementWords: is a draft, It's only as true as the board behind it

beats.role_note: SHOW-DON'T-TELL: the AI writes a confident green status; green is a judgment, not a fact
beats.narration_text: So here's the situation. Every tool now has a summarize-this-sprint button, and the paragraph it gives you is genuinely good writing -- clear, confident, ready to send. That's the trap. The AI sets the status to green by counting closed tickets. But green isn't a fact -- it's a judgment about whether you'll actually make it. The AI can't see the vendor who's gone quiet, the engineer who's out, the call that moved the deadline. As a time-saver, it's a gift. As the truth, it's a liability.

shot.visual_intent: AI generates a status card with a green ON TRACK badge + smooth prose lines; a traffic light the AI has set to GREEN. Then the real signal is revealed as AMBER behind it (hidden: vendor quiet, engineer out, deadline moved). Reframe: time-saver (gift) vs the truth (liability). Terracotta on the reframe.

beats.role_note: framework-first (PROOF): the 3 checks, shown BEFORE any example
beats.narration_text: So before you forward anything the AI wrote, verify three things. One: is it sourced? Every claim should point to something real on the board -- a closed ticket, an actual date -- not smooth prose filling a gap. Two: is it current? A status is only as true as the board behind it, and the AI will happily summarize a board nobody's touched in two weeks. Three: is it complete? The most important line is usually the one that isn't logged anywhere -- the blocker in a Slack thread, the risk from a call. Three checks pass, you sign it. Any check fails, you fix it first.

shot.visual_intent: Three checks stacked: 1 SOURCED? (points to a real ticket vs confident filler) 2 CURRENT? (board fresh vs stale) 3 COMPLETE? (off-board truth added vs missing). Each with a green pass test and a red failure. Footer rule: 3 PASS -> SIGN & SEND | any FAIL -> fix first. Terracotta on the footer.

beats.role_note: ASK->RESULT LAW -- composer ask that generates the T05 draft
beats.narration_text: Let's run a real one. Here's the end of a sprint. Watch me ask the AI to draft the status -- but only to draft it. Pull what's on the board into a clean update. Don't decide if we're on track, and don't invent anything.

props.command: Draft a sprint status update from my board for the client. Pull straight from the tickets -- what's done, in progress, and blocked. Don't declare on-track or at-risk, and don't add anything that isn't on the board. Mark anything you're unsure about.

beats.role_note: worked example walked through the framework -- verified, then the human adds COMPLETE
beats.narration_text: And there's the draft -- eight of ten tickets closed, two in progress, written up cleanly. Now verify it. Sourced? Yes, every line matches a real ticket. Current? Yes, I updated the board this morning. Complete? Almost -- and this is the part only I can do. The export feature depends on a vendor API that's been flaky all week, and that's on no card anywhere. I add one line flagging it as a risk. Now it's sourced, current, and complete. I sign it, and I send it.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the AI draft status card (8/10 closed, 2 in progress). Apply stamps: SOURCED check, CURRENT check. Then the HUMAN adds one line -- 'Risk: export depends on a flaky vendor API' -- and COMPLETE check lands -> a green SIGNED & SENT verdict. Green accent on the sign-off.

beats.role_note: falsifiability -- the confident all-green report that fails all three checks
beats.narration_text: Now the trap -- because a clean green report is so easy to forward. Same button, different sprint. The AI writes: project on track, all green. Looks perfect. Verify it. Sourced? No -- on track is the AI's guess from counting tickets; the board never says it. Current? No -- nobody's touched this board in ten days, because the team quietly moved to a hotfix. So the AI is summarizing a fossil. Complete? No -- the real blocker, a key engineer out sick, is nowhere on it. Three fails. Forward that, and you've told your client a confident lie. The test is what catches it before you do.

shot.visual_intent: A confident 'ON TRACK - all green' status card, then three RED stamps land: UNSOURCED (the AI's guess, not on the board), STALE (board untouched 10 days -> a fossil), INCOMPLETE (key engineer out, not logged) -> a red DO NOT SEND verdict. Terracotta/red on the failures.

beats.role_note: reusable rubric restated -- AI DRAFTS, you SIGN (sourced/current/complete)
beats.narration_text: So here's the rule you can carry to any tool. Let the AI draft -- it reads the board and writes the prose faster than you ever will. But you sign it. And your signature means you checked three things: that every claim is sourced, that the board is current, and that you added what the AI couldn't see. The AI writes the paragraph. You write the one line that actually matters.

shot.visual_intent: A clean router: LEFT 'AI DRAFTS -- reads the board, writes the prose'. A center gate = the three checks SOURCED / CURRENT / COMPLETE. RIGHT 'YOU SIGN -- send it to the stakeholder'. High negative space, terracotta accent on the signature gate.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW -- ClaudeComposerAsk 'Your turn.'; prompt read aloud + discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time your tool offers to write your status, don't just copy it out. Run this prompt: have the AI draft the update, but make it tag every single claim with the exact ticket or date it came from -- and separately list everything it could not verify from the board alone. Read that second list closely. That's your verification checklist, handed to you. A good answer gives you a sourced draft plus an honest here's-what-I-couldn't-see. A bad one gives a confident paragraph with no sources -- and now you know that's the one never to forward.

props.segment: Run it on your own status
props.command:
Draft my sprint/project status from the board below.
[PASTE YOUR BOARD]

1. SOURCED: tag every claim with the exact ticket ID or date it came from.
2. SEPARATE: list everything you canNOT verify from the board alone
   (on-track / at-risk judgments, off-board risks, anything stale).
3. Do NOT declare on-track or at-risk yourself -- leave that to me.
Give me (a) the sourced draft and (b) the 'could not verify' list.
